notes.claim: Wind-farm inter-array cables run from a turbine to the offshore substation, and a 66 kV array cable carries two times the power of a 33 kV one, according to one maker.
Every test starts from the same safe sequence: identify, isolate, prove dead, secure and earth. The earths come off only under control for a test, and go back on at the end.
IEC 60502-2 covers extruded-insulation cables only up to 30 kV, so it does not cover a 66 kV cable such as String B.

A conductor that has been disconnected can still be charged. HSE counts a conductor as charged if it picked up charge by induction or kept or regained charge through capacitance effects while disconnected.
Your notes say nearby energised circuits can induce voltage into an isolated cable, so a disconnected cable is treated as live until it has been tested, discharged and earthed.
HSE says equipment that stores charge, such as high-voltage cables, must have the charge safely discharged, and that local earths at the point of work go on only after proving dead there.

The regulations require isolation to be secure, and precautions to stop dead equipment from becoming charged during the work. HSE guidance says isolation includes guarding against charge by induction or capacitance effects.
The voltage indicator used to prove dead is itself proved immediately before and immediately after testing the conductors.
Your notes warn that the energy stored in the insulation can recharge the conductor after it has been discharged, and Megger says that absorbed energy takes a while to release.
Your notes give the shock factors as voltage, resistance, path and duration, with body resistance about 10,000 Ω at 55 V and 50 mA or more potentially fatal.
A long cable has significant capacitance. For a three-core 66 kV XLPE submarine cable at 240 mm², ABB lists 0.22 µF/km and 2.6 A/km charging current per phase at 50 Hz, in its 66 kV table.

A real three-core submarine design can carry a lead metallic screen and steel armour over the cores, which the notes' layer list leaves out. The oversheath can have a protective function for the insulation.

A maker's three-core medium-voltage submarine cable lists, middle out: conductor screen, XLPE insulation, insulation screen, swelling tape, copper wires, laminated aluminium tape and a PE or semi-conductive PE outer sheath, so your notes' layer list matches a real build; the same maker's lead-sheath version has a lead sheath instead of the wires and foil. Armour comes over the cores.

U0 is the rated voltage between the conductor and earth or the metal screen. For a 72.5 kV highest voltage, one maker names the cable 38/66 (72.5) kV while a rated-voltage table in another pairs 72.5 kV with U0 = 36 kV, so U0 is read from the cable's own data sheet (the case uses 38 kV, a practice value).

The body's impedance is not a fixed number. It varies with the touch voltage, path, duration, skin moisture, contact area and temperature, and it falls as voltage rises because the skin breaks down at a few hundred volts. Your notes' 10 000 Ω at 55 V is the notes' figure; no source here gives a value at 55 V, so the sourced point is the direction, not the number.

The effects thresholds: about 0.5 mA to react, about 10 mA AC as the let-go threshold for adult males (5 mA for the whole population), and ventricular fibrillation at 50 mA for a one-second shock, falling to 40 mA beyond 3 s. Your notes put 50 mA or more as potentially fatal.

For a screened cable the coupling that matters is inductive. It lands on all the metal parts of the cable, in or out of service (armour, sheath, conductor), depends on the neighbour's current, the distance and the length of parallelism, and not on the neighbour's voltage. So your notes' 'the longer the worse' holds for this.

Capacitive coupling forms a voltage divider, so part of a live neighbour's voltage appears on an unearthed conductor. But overhead lines and busbars influence only conductors not screened by earth or an earthed screen, and offshore cables hold their field inside the shielded insulation. So the 'capacitor beside a live one' picture shows the divider idea and the stored charge, not a real coupling figure for a screened core. For two overhead lines the capacitive voltage does not depend on the parallel length.

The rule that follows: a disconnected cable's sheath and core are shunted and earthed locally to prevent a standing voltage, and dangerous voltages can arrive unpredictably from faults, switching or lightning even when it is safe under normal conditions.

'Impressed voltages' is the term for induced or capacitive voltage on metalwork, and 'trapped charge' is residual charge left on the capacitance of equipment, for example after insulation resistance testing a length of cable.

A high-voltage cable should be treated as a capacitor that can store energy, and its capacitance is easy to overlook when disconnecting it. The energy in a capacitor is ½CV². A capacitor can also recharge a few minutes after the shorting device is removed (dielectric absorption), which is why the earth stays on.
A breaker opens a capacitive current as it passes through zero, which falls near the peak of the voltage, so the cable is left charged near its peak.
Your notes call under 1 Ω low resistance, and list lead resistance, contact resistance and external influences as what disturbs such readings.
A four-wire low-resistance meter uses separate current and voltage leads, so the voltage is measured at the device and lead and contact resistance drop out of the reading.
The two potential probes must face each other, which keeps them inside the current connections. Your notes name the Megger DLRO10HD for this work.
Megger describes the standard method for a cable core as connecting the current and potential leads at each end of the core.
Phase identification starts with the cable earthed at both ends and uses the colour code red L1, yellow L2, blue L3, proved by core-to-screen continuity from both ends.
Measured core resistance should be within 2% of the factory values, and any deviation is explained before the results are submitted.
Your notes need a technician at each end: closing the earth switch or fitting test adapters at the HV terminations completes the circuit, and the sequence moves links and earths step by step.
Copper's temperature coefficient of resistance at 20 °C is given as 0.00393 per °C by two maker pages, so copper's resistance changes with temperature.

Megger colours the DLRO10HD range switch: the yellow band holds the test current, the green ranges limit the output power to 0.25 W, and the red ranges are the high-power ones that dissipate up to 25 W into the test piece.
On the DLRO10HD the 1 A range at 2.5 W reads up to 2.5 Ω and the 10 A range at 25 W up to 250 mΩ, so a loop of about 340 mΩ is beyond the 10 A range and sits on the 1 A one.
The DLRO10HD reverses the current and averages the readings, which cancels thermal EMFs. Its voltmeter input impedance is above 200 kΩ, and the maximum lead resistance at 10 A is under 100 mΩ.
On the sample the potential probes face each other and the current connections sit outside them. The value read is the resistance between the two potential points.
No current flows in the P leads, so neither their resistance nor the resistance of the P contacts adds a voltage to the reading.
A two-wire reading adds the total lead resistance to the result, which is why a low-resistance reading needs four wires.
Noise induced into the leads can disturb a low-resistance reading. The DLRO10HD flashes a noise icon and shows no result above 100 mV at 50 or 60 Hz.

The standard temperature coefficient of copper is 0.00393 per °C at 20 °C. IEC 60228 sets its resistance limits at 20 °C and has measured resistance corrected to 20 °C by the factors in its Table A.1.
A copper class 2 conductor of 240 mm² has a maximum of 0.0754 Ω/km at 20 °C (bare wires). Over String B's 2.40 km that is at most 181 mΩ a core.

A utility's commissioning procedure measures conductor d.c. loop resistance to show the conductor joints and terminations are effective, and compares the result with the manufacturer's resistance in ohms per kilometre.

After work that could disturb the phasing, the phasing must be proved by testing. On a three-phase cable each conductor is tested in turn with the screen as the return, and phase-to-phase tests are not required. Another utility checks phase identification with phasing resistors or a continuity check of each core after jointing.
Good insulation shows rising resistance during the test as the charging currents disappear, while in poor insulation high leakage current hides them and the curve is much flatter.
The dielectric absorption ratio is the ratio of two time-resistance readings, such as 60 s over 30 s. The polarization index is the 10-minute reading over the 1-minute reading.
Both ratios are taken on the same equipment minutes apart, and Megger says they can be seen as independent of temperature. Your notes add that a single reading swings with conditions.
Healthy insulation shows rising resistance over time. A low or unstable PI can indicate moisture, contamination or insulation breakdown.
Your notes rate PI below 1 poor, 1 to 2 questionable, 2 to 4 okay and above 4 good, and DAR below 1.25 inadequate, 1.25 to 1.6 satisfactory and above 1.6 excellent.
Makers' bands differ from the notes' names and cut-offs, so the client's criteria decide pass or fail.
notes.contested: Your notes rate PI 1 to 2 questionable and DAR 1.25 to 1.6 satisfactory. A Megger Q&A says PI of 2.0 or higher and DAR of 1.4 or higher indicate good insulation, and Megger accepts PI of 1 to 2 for very low-capacitance equipment.

notes.claim: Megger says the DAR reading is usually lower than the PI reading because its test times are shorter.
Your notes pass an IR test if the voltage is held for the full duration and the resistance exceeds the client's criteria, and say to default to PI or DAR when possible.
After the test the cable is discharged: check the device display, use the discharge stick, then the hook stick, then apply earths to core and screen. Your notes allow 5 times the charging time.
notes.contested: Your notes say to allow 5 times the charging time to discharge, without defining it. Megger's guide says to discharge for about four times as long as the test voltage was applied.

notes.claim: Megger's guide gives the discharge time as about four times as long as the test voltage was applied in a previous test.

Megger's guide says to discharge the item under test for five times as long as it was tested, and gives the example of a 10-minute PI test, which needs 50 minutes. A Fluke application note says about five times the testing charge time.
Megger's guide says to short out a tested item firmly after discharge until it is needed, because stored absorption charge can be released afterwards and raise the voltage to dangerous levels.

Megger's guide uses charging time in a second sense, the time the test set takes to charge the sample, which follows from the sample's capacitance. It is a separate idea from the five times rule, which counts the time the voltage was applied.
notes.contested: Your notes say five times the charging time without defining it. Megger's newer guide says five times as long as the item was tested, with 50 minutes after a 10-minute PI test, and a Fluke application note says about five times the testing charge time. Megger's older guide says about four times. The lesson uses five times the time the voltage was applied.

notes.claim: Megger puts the positive terminal on the grounded outside of a cable, so the negative lead goes to the conductor. For a plain IR test it says polarity rarely matters, but on older insulation electroendosmosis gives a lower reading when the positive terminal is on the grounded side.
The current in an IR test is a charging current and an absorption current, which fall to negligible values, and a small steady leakage current that is left.

A single IR reading falls markedly as temperature rises, with a rule of thumb of halving for every 10 degrees C. A time-resistance ratio such as PI is relatively independent of temperature and needs no past records.
A PI or DAR close to 1 means the insulation is judged to have deteriorated.
Some materials show very little or no dielectric absorption, and a high PI above 5 may point to brittle or cracked insulation, so a PI is read with the material in mind.
IEEE 43 (a rotating-machine practice) says the PI test is not recommended as an assessment tool when the 1-minute reading is above 5000 megohms. A long XLPE cable can read far above that.
notes.contested: Your notes and Megger use PI on cables with no upper limit. IEEE 43 is written for rotating machines, not cables, and a Fluke note says cabling shows little absorption current. The lesson teaches PI as the notes do, flags that a very high 1-minute reading makes the ratio hard to trust, and leans on the client's criterion and the trend.

notes.claim: Megger's Table I rates DAR (60/30 s) 1.0 to 1.25 questionable, 1.4 to 1.6 good and above 1.6 excellent, with a gap between 1.25 and 1.4, and PI below 1 dangerous, 1 to 2 questionable, 2 to 4 good and above 4 excellent. A Megger Q&A calls PI of 2.0 or higher and DAR of 1.4 or higher good.
notes.contested: Your notes name the PI bands poor, questionable, okay, good and set DAR at 1.25 and 1.6 with no gap. Megger's names and DAR cut-offs differ. Teach the notes' bands for the practice, show Megger's as a maker's view, and let the client's criterion settle pass or fail.

notes.claim: Megger says diagnostic testers for medium-voltage cables, machines and transformers normally have outputs of 5 or 10 kV, so a 5 kV IR test on a 66 kV cable is a normal diagnostic test voltage.
Every insulation test starts from fully discharged insulation.
IEC 60229 sets a site test of 4 kV d.c. per millimetre of specified oversheath thickness, at most 10 kV, for 1 minute, between the underlying metallic layers and an outer electrode.
In that standard all metallic layers under the oversheath are connected together, and no breakdown of the oversheath may occur during the test.
The factory routine test in IEC 60229 is stronger: 8 kV d.c. per millimetre for 1 minute, with the underlying metal layer at negative polarity.
Your notes give the same test: screen conductor to earth, 4 kV per mm of sheath thickness up to 10 kV for 1 minute, with conductor, foil and screen connected together.
Your notes say lots of cables have sheath faults, which can cause full cable loss and be very expensive.
IEC 60229 notes that an oversheath can be designed to protect the insulation as well as against corrosion, which is why its integrity matters.

For a sheath that is not semi-conductive, your notes connect negative to the screen conductor and positive to an earth electrode. For a semi-conductive sheath, positive goes through a roll spring to the semi-con layer.
One utility specification calls for a 10 kV d.c. test for 1 minute between sheath and earth where the outer sheath is insulating rather than semi-conducting.
A damaged sheath lets water in. Water that passes through a damaged sheath or joint causes water treeing once the electric field acts on it.

The outer jacket slows the ingress of water and ions from outside. Water trees are tiny branching cavities that grow slowly, over months or years, until the stress at a tip starts an electrical tree and the cable faults. Moisture, a high field, insulation defects and time together promote them.

A utility's guide names failure of the enclosing sheath, and the ingress of water, as a major cause of cable failure, and says actual failure does not come straight after the breach. A commissioning-test review of HV cable says failures are more often due to sheath problems than to the main insulation. That is why a sheath that fails its test matters while the main insulation still passes.

Sheath test levels differ by who sets them: the notes and IEC 60229 give 4 kV per mm up to 10 kV for 1 minute. A distribution network operator uses 10 kV DC for 1 minute on new installation of insulated-sheath cable and 5 kV for 1 minute on 6.6 to 33 kV polymeric cable. A cable maker's guide for medium-voltage cable uses a 1000 V insulation test. Taught as different levels for different cables, with the case using the notes' rule.

The IEC standards for 30 to 500 kV cable (IEC 60840 and IEC 62067) limit their after-installation tests to withstand tests on the main insulation and the sheath. IEC 60840 covers 66 kV cable but leaves submarine cables out of its scope, saying the standard tests may need modifying for them. So the oversheath rule in the notes is the notes' and IEC 60229's, applied to a subsea cable by the course.

The outer face of the sheath needs a conductor for the test voltage to cross the sheath. On land cable a graphite or semi-conducting coating on the sheath gives a continuous potential. A submarine functional specification asks for graphite or an extruded conductive layer on the polyethylene outer sheath to facilitate DC testing of the outer sheath. Voltage goes between the ungrounded screen and the ground, so the screen's earth is taken off for the test.

In a three-core 66 kV array cable each power core has its own polyethylene sheath over its screen. The armour wires and outer polypropylene yarn serving sit outside the three cores. So the sheath test of a three-core cable is made on each core's sheath; no source here describes testing the outer yarn serving, which is open to seawater.

Sheath test sets are made with 10 kV DC outputs of either polarity. The maker's manual says the test object is discharged by the set's discharge device after the test and must be earthed before any contact.

After a sheath test the screens need earthing for time before handling: a cable maker's guide says at least 5 minutes after a sheath insulation test. A case from a 132 kV line is where the screen earths were not put back after the sheath tests and the line ran energised for several days without them.

Your notes say a mains-frequency HV withstand test needs very high power because of cable capacitance, and that lowering the frequency raises the capacitive reactance and cuts the power and current needed.
The power needed to energise a cable capacitance is proportional to test frequency. One source gives 500 times less energy at 0.1 Hz than at 50 Hz, another 600 times less power than at 60 Hz.
Traditional 50/60 Hz testing was impractical on site because of the strong capacitive nature of cables.
DC testing built up space charge that accelerated water tree growth in healthy XLPE. VLF reverses polarity, which reduces that build-up but is still a compromise.
IEEE 400.2 covers VLF below 1 Hz, most commonly 0.1 Hz, with recommended test voltages for installation, acceptance and maintenance.
The VLF test range is taught as contested: the notes give 1.5 to 2.5 U0, while the IEEE guide as reproduced by High Voltage Inc bases installation and acceptance levels on practice of up to 3 U0.
notes.contested: Your notes give 1.5 to 2.5 U0 for installation, acceptance and maintenance. IEEE 400.2 as reproduced by High Voltage Inc bases installation and acceptance on practice of from less than 2 U0 to 3 U0, with maintenance about 75% of acceptance.

notes.claim: U0 is the rated rms phase-to-ground voltage. IEEE 400.2 Table 3 (sinusoidal, 69 kV class) as reproduced by High Voltage Inc lists 75, 84 and 63 kV rms for installation, acceptance and maintenance.
Recommended minimum time is 60 min at 0.1 Hz for installation or acceptance on new cable, and 30 min for a simple withstand on aged cable. The notes list the same durations.

A VLF withstand test excites any defect large enough at the test voltage, which triggers partial discharge in it. Your notes add that a severe defect starts an electrical tree that grows in the insulation.
Terminations may need to be added to avoid flashover for installation tests on cables rated above 35 kV.
Long cables need a lower frequency, a lower voltage or both, but lowering the frequency needlessly is to be avoided. A pass means the voltage held for the full duration with no breakdown.
Your notes call VLF an AC hi-potential test at a lower frequency, run at 0.1 and 0.01 Hz, and end it by applying the discharge stick, then the hook, then the hand earth.
ABB lists 0.22 µF/km and 2.6 A/km at 50 Hz for a three-core 66 kV XLPE submarine cable of 240 mm².

A VLF set is rated by the load capacitance it can test at each frequency, and the lower the frequency the longer the cable it can test. A 0.75 µF set at 0.1 Hz takes twice that load at 0.05 Hz. One 200 kV peak set is listed at 0.75 µF at 0.1 Hz up to 3.75 µF at 0.02 Hz; a 120 kV peak set at 0.55 µF at 0.1 Hz.
A set should run at 0.1 Hz unless the cable is too big a load for its rating there. A full cycle at 0.1 Hz takes 10 seconds, 20 seconds at 0.05 Hz and 50 seconds at 0.02 Hz.

VLF sets are rated in kV peak, and a sine wave's rms is 0.707 of its peak. IEEE 400.2 Table 3 gives the 69 kV class installation level as 75 kV rms (106 kV peak). The largest 0.1 Hz sets reach about 200 kV peak.

The defect picture: a defect big enough to be excited by the applied voltage grows to failure during the test, and lesser defects are not affected. Time can be shortened to 15 to 30 minutes if the monitored characteristic stays stable and nothing fails, against the 60 minute recommendation.

U0 is the rated rms power frequency voltage between conductor and earth or metallic screen. In a rating such as 38/66 (72.5) kV, 38 kV is U0, 66 kV is U between conductors and 72.5 kV is the highest system voltage Um.
DC withstand testing of extruded cable has been discouraged by IEEE 400.1, ICEA S-94-649 and IEC 60502-2; DC can induce space charge in XLPE that contributes to degradation.

After any high-voltage test an XLPE cable holds charge in its capacitance and its dielectric. Residual voltage can persist for minutes or even hours and voltage can rebound after a first discharge, so discharge with a stick, apply a direct ground and keep it connected, then measure the residual voltage before anyone gets access. Test at 2 U0 or 2.5 U0 raises the stored energy, which grows with the square of the voltage.

Whether VLF suits a 66 kV inter-array cable is contested. The notes and IEEE 400.2 (a guide for cables rated 5 kV to 69 kV) support a 0.1 Hz VLF withstand; but a test-system maker reads IEC 63026 as requiring 10 to 500 Hz for commissioning cables above 36 kV, and 66 kV array strings have been commissioned with resonant AC sets per IEC 63026. CIGRE TB 490 says a lower frequency down to 10 Hz can be acceptable for long submarine cables. The IEC 63026 clause text is paywalled and was not seen.
notes.contested: Your notes and IEEE 400.2 teach a 0.1 Hz VLF withstand as the field test; a test-system maker says IEC 63026 asks for 10 to 500 Hz on cables above 36 kV, and resonant AC sets are used on 66 kV array strings. The clause itself was not seen, so the client's specification settles it.

notes.claim: A TDR uses the radar principle: a pulse goes down the cable and changes in impedance send reflections back, which are displayed as a map of the cable.
A positive reflection shows a higher impedance and a negative one a lower impedance, because conductors moving apart or closer together change the impedance.
An open conductor shows a large positive trace and a short circuit a negative trace. A joint shows a small positive followed by a small negative trace.
A wet splice or water gives a short positive and negative trace, and your notes list a ragged trailing section for water ingress.

The velocity factor is the ratio of the pulse speed in the cable to the speed of light, and it must be set for the cable. If unknown, test a known length and adjust it until the displayed end distance is correct.
Megger lists a velocity factor of 0.54 to 0.62, which is 162 to 186 m per microsecond, for power XLPE cable.
Distance comes from the time of the reflected pulse times the velocity, taking half of the time, because the pulse goes to the fault and back. Your notes write L = t × v ÷ 2.
If the velocity factor is wrong for the cable, the displayed distance will be wrong.

A clear open reflection is not necessarily the end of the cable, because it can also be a break or cut, so the end is proved with open and linked tests. Linked gives a negative peak, open a positive one.
TDR needs two separate conductive elements, one of which may be the armour or screen. Your notes say two conductors in parallel, a fixed 50 V pulse, and shorter pulse width for shorter cables.
Testing from both ends and recording the distance to fault helps work out how wide a problem is, and after water the velocity factor changes, so readings past the water may be wrong.
Your notes say TDR only works on low resistance faults, typically under 100 Ω (200 Ω for Teleflex), with accuracy of 0 to 1% of cable length.

The reflection coefficient is rho = (Z load - Z0) ÷ (Z load + Z0): the reflected pulse divided by the pulse sent. It runs from +1 for an open to -1 for a short, with 0 for a matched load that reflects nothing.
A positive reflection means the impedance rose, a negative one that it fell. A matched end absorbs the whole pulse, so the cable looks endless and no end reflection comes back.

Z0 = square root of (L per length ÷ C per length), and the velocity factor is 1 ÷ the square root of the relative permittivity. A cable's L and C per length follow from its Z0 and its velocity, so Z0 = 1 ÷ (v × C per length): used for the practice value for String B, 27.1 ohm from 168.0 m/µs and 0.22 µF/km, close to the 25 ohm a Megger TDR sets for power cable.

A fault of resistance Rf from core to screen sits across the line as a shunt, so the pulse sees Rf in parallel with Z0 and the reflection is rho = -Z0 ÷ (2 Rf + Z0). It falls steadily as Rf rises and has no cliff at 100 ohm; the notes' 100 ohm is where it gets too small to read. This is worked from the quoted reflection coefficient and the parallel rule, not quoted as such.

Megger says a fault below 100 ohm can be found with a low-voltage TDR pulse (it gives 40 V as an example), and that above 100 ohm the pulse will likely not see it. This agrees with the notes' 'under about 100 ohm'. A higher-resistance fault is not seen by TDR; the arc reflection method strikes an arc at the fault with a surge generator, the arc behaves like a short for the TDR, and the arc trace is compared with a reference trace taken first. Named, not taught.

Pulse amplitude depends on the set: Megger's Teleflex SX-1 is 50 V fixed (as in the notes) its Teleflex VX is 30 to 160 V, and a hand-held TDR500 gives 5 V peak to peak. A TDR must only go on a de-energised, isolated cable; the TDR500 manual says it is not to be used on energised cable, and the CFL510G guide says the circuit must be switched off, de-energised, securely isolated and proved safe before test connections are made.

The Teleflex takes the velocity as v/2 (half the pulse speed): Megger writes that in TDR analyses the velocity is always given in v/2, and its range is quoted at v/2 = 80 m/µs and settable from 10 to 149.9 m/µs. A set that asks for v/2 needs 84.0 where the notes' formula L = t × v ÷ 2 uses v = 168.0.
If the velocity setting is out by 2 per cent, every distance is out by 2 per cent. With the cable's length known, the velocity is found by moving it until the end sits at the known length.

From both ends, the two distances to one fault should add up to the cable's length: the TDR500 manual says the combined answer should equal the expected length, and a maker's example (2050 ft from one end and 3075 ft from the other on a 5000 ft cable) shows the velocity set too fast.

Record a TDR reference trace (fingerprint) when the cable is commissioned. Joints give reflections that can be taken for a fault, so the joints' places should be known on the trace beforehand; sheath-sectionalised joints can also mislead. The length of a submarine cable reduces TDR accuracy, so the velocity along the whole length matters. The trace records joints as well as faults.

A wider pulse reaches further and shows smaller faults but has a bigger blind spot next to the instrument, so start with the shortest pulse; the notes' 'shorter cable, shorter pulse'. The blind-spot lengths published are for telephone cable, so no figure for String B is taken from them.

Velocity is not one number for all XLPE: Megger's 162 to 186 m/µs (0.54 to 0.62) is typical. Temperature barely moves it at ambient (about 0.034 per cent per degree) but near the 90 °C operating limit it is 0.56 per cent per degree, so set the velocity from a known length at the cable's own temperature.
The speed of light is exactly 299 792 458 m/s, 299.8 m/µs to 4 figures, so a velocity factor is the velocity in m/µs divided by 299.8.

Accuracy: the notes say TDR is generally accurate to 0-1% of the cable's length. A maker states accuracy as a percentage of the range, at one velocity factor, and only if the velocity factor is right.
LIRA is based on transmission line theory: it estimates and analyses the complex line impedance as a function of signal frequency, and measures the surge impedance over a wide range of frequencies.
Your notes say LIRA needs access to only one end, works on frequency-domain resonance effects of unmatched lines, and is sensitive to small changes in insulation permittivity.
Changes in dielectric permittivity change the cable impedance. A damaged segment differs mainly through a change in cable capacitance.

Joints, splices or defects create a deviation in the input impedance spectrum. The resonance frequencies give the cable length and the phase spectrum shows condition and locates joints and degradation.
Wirescan's patent gives the relative phase velocity from two consecutive resonance frequencies: vr = 2L(fk+1 − fk)/v0, where L is the length of the cable and v0 is the speed of light.
LIRA works with any termination except an exact match to the cable impedance, which makes the cable look endless.
DNORM indicates the severity of local impedance changes, and its sign helps determine the type of change.
DNORM normalises the spike difference from the terminal peak, and a local spot has a mirror image beyond the terminal peak from a second-order reflection.

Your notes give a negative DNORM for thermal degradation, water penetration and mechanical causes, and positive for bends and breaks in the shield. Colours run green mild, amber intermediate, red significant.
Your notes say tests are normally bi-directional, take about a minute each, run to 18 tests of core to screen and core to core, have no acceptance criteria, and need the raw trace data kept.
Wirescan's patent says LIRA can estimate the location of a degraded spot to within 0.5% of the cable length.
Both ends are earthed and discharged before a LIRA test so no energy is stored in the cable.
